metadata.title: What makes teachers stay? A cross-sectional exploration of the individual and contextual factors associated with teacher retention in Sweden.

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses a Swedish questionnaire dataset collected by AFA-insurance from municipality elementary-year teachers (25 municipalities). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analysis is based on a cross-sectional sample of qualified teachers with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria (public schools; permanent contracts; ISCED 1–2), the results should be interpreted as associations within this sampled population rather than as ILSA-style nationally representative estimates with documented design weights. For replication, analysts should verify whether AFA-insurance provided any sampling/selection weights; if none exist, standard unweighted regression assumptions apply.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is teachers’ retention intention measured via a single-item 3-point prognosis question from the Work Ability Index (WAI-6), not a cognitive achievement score with plausible values. Therefore, plausible values are not applicable because there is no PV-based achievement scaling in this dataset. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap for transparency about how incomplete questionnaires were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used AFA-insurance questionnaire data collected between 2004 and 2011 from municipality workers in Sweden. Included only qualified elementary-year teachers (ISCED level 1–2) working in public schools; excluded teachers with temporary employment contracts (to avoid job-insecurity-driven turnover) and excluded unqualified teachers. The final analytic sample consists of 5903 teachers from 25 municipalities; the paper notes that the sample is representative of the Swedish teacher population by age, formal qualifications, and gender, and geographically representative across municipality groups.

main_findings.dataset_used: Sweden AFA-insurance teacher questionnaire (2004–2011), elementary-year teachers (ISCED 1–2), public schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression (model 4): total R² = 0.202 (F(14, 4415) = 81.2, p < .001). Final significant standardized predictors: health-related quality of life (b = 0.29, p < .001), exhaustion (b = -0.14, p < .001), work motivation (b = 0.10, p < .001), support from colleagues (b = 0.06, p < .001), work-life interference (b = 0.05, p < .05), organizational commitment (b = 0.04, p < .05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Sweden AFA-insurance teacher questionnaire data (2004–2011) for elementary-year teachers in public schools, the study leveraged health-related quality of life, exhaustion, work motivation, support from colleagues, and work-life interference to predict teachers’ retention intention, finding that better perceived health and higher motivation were associated with greater retention intention while exhaustion and higher work-life interference were associated with lower retention intention. This indicates that strengthening teacher health-promoting working conditions and sustaining motivation—alongside fostering collegial support—may improve retention intentions, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-sectional study analyzed AFA-insurance questionnaire data collected in Sweden between 2004 and 2011 from 5903 qualified elementary-year teachers (ISCED 1–2) working in public schools across 25 municipalities. Teachers’ retention intention was measured using the WAI-6 item (a 3-point prognosis about being able to continue in the profession two years later). The authors used hierarchical multiple regression (with stepwise/backward selection for exploratory model building) rather than machine learning, and found that individual-level factors explained most of the variance in retention intention, with the final hierarchical model explaining R² = 0.202 (F(14, 4415) = 81.2, p < .001). The strongest standardized associations were health-related quality of life (b = 0.29, p < .001) and exhaustion (b = -0.14, p < .001), followed by work motivation (b = 0.10, p < .001) and support from colleagues (b = 0.06, p < .001). Limitations include reliance on self-report and the absence of reported missing-data handling; causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional design.
